scenes.label: Meet the team
scenes.title: A bulletin needs sorting
scenes.caption: Aditi brings fictional bulletin cards into the Decision Lab. Vihaan first writes the purpose: help a volunteer find workshop notices. The output is a workshop label for each card, with a person checking before posting.

scenes.label: The problem
scenes.title: A rule can be inspected
scenes.caption: Their baseline marks a card positive whenever its text contains workshop. On cards A through F, it predicts yes, yes, no, no, yes, no. The checked labels are yes, no, yes, no, yes, no.

scenes.label: How it works
scenes.title: A different candidate
scenes.caption: The supplied model predicts yes, no, yes, no, no, no on those same cards. Aditi circles its disagreement on E. A model can improve the total while still introducing a mistake that the simple rule avoided.

scenes.label: Your decision
scenes.title: Keep the comparison fair
scenes.caption: Vihaan suggests giving the model easier cards. Aditi stops the comparison: the target, checked labels and cases must stay fixed. Choose a plan that measures both methods under equivalent conditions, including the volunteer’s available review time.

scenes.label: What changes
scenes.title: Count paired errors
scenes.caption: The rule is wrong on B and C; the model is wrong on E. Their error counts are 2 and 1. These supplied predictions support a narrow pack comparison, without showing how the model learned its behaviour.

scenes.title: Return to usefulness
scenes.caption: They attach the evidence to the purpose card. Review effort, missed notices and whether sorting helps volunteers still need investigation. Aditi keeps the baseline available while the notebook distinguishes prediction quality from a useful, appropriate application.
